narrative: The model estimates a 61% probability that you will leave, meaning it expects departure more than staying. Because the promotion decision relied on that forecast, you are being denied promotion now—not because your work was judged insufficient, but because the organization is treating you as a retention risk. The strongest signal was that you reported having other job opportunities while in this job. Only about a quarter of employees predicted to stay had such opportunities, so this uncommon factor pushed the forecast most strongly toward leaving. The second signal was the amount of training you attended in the last three years: one to three programs. This level was the second-strongest contributor and leaned toward leaving. Third was your experience profile: six to ten years overall and six to ten years in this organization. Among employees predicted to stay, half have only one to five years overall and about a third have six to ten, so your mid-tenure position also nudged the forecast toward departure. Your recognition, satisfaction, stability and commitment may count in the other direction, but they did not outweigh these signals. Next, you and the organization should discuss your intentions and career path openly. The organization should clarify promotion criteria, retention options, development and training plans; you should assess whether this role still meets your goals.
